question.text: Simplify the expression $( A \land B) \lor (A\land \neg B).$
question.explanation:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operations:

  • First, we use the distributive law (conjunction over disjunction): \[ ( A \land B) \lor (A\land \neg B) \equiv A \land (B \lor \neg B) \]

  • Next, we use the fact that the disjunction of an expression and its negation is a tautology: \[ A \land ({\color{blue}B \lor \neg B}) \equiv A \land {\color{blue}\textbf{t}} \]

  • Finally, we use the fact that the conjunction of an expression and a tautology gives the initial expression: \[ A \land \textbf{t} \equiv A \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ ( A \land B) \lor (A\land \neg B) \equiv A. \]

  • First, we use that $X \Rightarrow Y \equiv \neg X \lor Y {:}$ \[ (P \land Q)\land ({\color{blue} P \Rightarrow \neg Q}) \equiv (P \land Q)\land ({\color{blue} \neg P \lor \neg Q}) \]

  • Next, we use a De Morgan's law: \[ (P \land Q)\land {\color{blue}( \neg P \lor \neg Q)} \equiv (P \land Q)\land {\color{blue} \neg (P \land Q)} \]

  • Finally, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and its negation is a contradiction: \[ (P \land Q)\land \neg (P \land Q) \equiv \mathbf c \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ (P \land Q)\land (P \Rightarrow \neg Q) \equiv \mathbf c. \]

question.text: Simplify the expression $\neg ( A \land \neg(B \land A)).$
question.explanation:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operations:

  • First, we use a De Morgan's law: \[ \neg ( A \land \neg(B \land A)) \equiv \neg A \lor \neg \neg (B \land A) \]

  • Next, we simplify the double negation: \[ \neg A \lor {\color{blue}\neg \neg} (B \land A) \equiv \neg A \lor (B \land A) \]

  • Then, we use the distributive law (disjunction over conjunction): \[ \neg A \lor (B \land A) \equiv (\neg A \lor B) \land (\neg A \lor A) \]

  • Then, we use the fact that the disjunction of an expression and its negation is a tautology: \[ (\neg A \lor B) \land ({\color{blue} \neg A \lor A }) \equiv (\neg A \lor B) \land {\color{blue} \textbf{t} } \]

  • Finally, we use the fact that the conjunction of an expression and a tautology gives the initial expression: \[ (\neg A \lor B) \land \textbf{t} \equiv \neg A \lor B \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ \neg ( A \land \neg(B \land A))\equiv \neg A \lor B. \]

question.text: Simplify the expression $\neg (A \Rightarrow B) \land \neg A.$
question.explanation:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

  • First, we use that $X \Rightarrow Y \equiv \neg X \lor Y {:}$ \[ \neg ({\color{blue}A \Rightarrow B}) \land \neg A \equiv \neg (\lnot A \lor B) \land \neg A \]

  • Next, we use a De Morgan's law: \[ {\color{blue}\neg (\lnot A \lor B) } \land \neg A \equiv {\color{blue}(\lnot\lnot A \land \lnot B)} \land \neg A \]

  • Then, we simplify the double negation: \[ ({\color{blue} \lnot\lnot} A \land \lnot B) \land \neg A \equiv ( A \land \lnot B) \land \neg A \]

  • Next, we use the commutative law: \[ ( {\color{blue}A \land \lnot B}) \land \neg A \equiv ({\color{blue} \lnot B \land A}) \land \neg A \]

  • Then, we use the associative law: \[ (\lnot B \land A) \land \neg A \equiv \lnot B \land ( A \land \neg A ) \]

  • Next, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and its negation is a contradiction: \[ \lnot B \land {\color{blue}( A \land \neg A )} \equiv \lnot B \land {\color{blue} \mathbf c} \]

  • Finally, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and a contradiction gives a contradiction: \[ \lnot B \land \mathbf c \equiv \mathbf c \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ \neg (A \Rightarrow B) \land \neg A \equiv \mathbf c. \]

question.text: Simplify the expression $\big[ A\land (\neg A \land B)\big] \land (A \lor B ).$
question.explanation:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

  • First, we use the associative law: \[ \big[ {\color{blue} A\land (\neg A \land B) } \big] \land (A \lor B ) \equiv \big[ {\color{blue} (A\land \neg A) \land B } \big] \land (A \lor B ) \]

  • Next, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and its negation is a contradiction: \[ \big[ {\color{blue} (A\land \neg A)} \land B \big] \land (A \lor B ) \equiv (\mathbf {\color{blue}{c}} \land B) \land (A \lor B ) \]

  • Then, we use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and a contradiction gives a contradiction: \[ {\color{blue} (\mathbf {c} \land B)} \land (A \lor B ) \equiv {\color{blue} \mathbf {c} } \land (A \lor B ) \]

  • Finally, we again use the fact that the conjunction of a statement and a contradiction gives a contradiction: \[ \mathbf {c} \land (A \lor B ) \equiv \mathbf {c} \]

Therefore, we conclude that \[ \big[ A\land (\neg A \land B) \big] \land (A \lor B ) \equiv \mathbf {c}. \]
